# Ian Zepp — A life in systems

Full text of https://ianzepp.dev/ as Markdown, for agent readers.
The HTML page is canonical; this file mirrors its content. Measurements are
dated July 12, 2026.

## I retired early. Then AI made me curious again.

I'm Ian Zepp: a software founder, former engineering executive, and lifelong
systems builder. This is the long version — the work, the pivots, the evidence,
and what happened when a career in enterprise software collided with a year of
nearly uninterrupted AI-assisted R&D.

The last year, measured: 218 local repositories, 17,710 deduplicated commits,
6,638 recorded agent sessions, and one 117-day unbroken streak. Every number on
the page keeps its measurement date. Currently building in Rust.

## A one-person lab, run at industrial pace (Sept 2025 — present)

For the last ten months I have done research and development full time with AI
agents: a programming language and its compiler, two agent runtimes, a
multi-tenant platform, MCP security tooling, and the evaluation harnesses that
keep all of it honest.

The claim worth examining is not the volume — it is the method. I have been
working out a repeatable way to direct, constrain, test, and audit AI-assisted
engineering: goals and invariants written down before code, work split into
bounded phases, commits used as checkpoints, and completion audited separately
from implementation.

### Measurements (July 12, 2026)

- 17,710 unique commits, Aug 2025 — Jul 2026
- 218 local Git repositories
- 6,638 recorded agent sessions
- 117 days, longest unbroken active streak
- 6,087 test definitions across six systems
- 17,681 LLM trial executions recorded

Commits are deduplicated by SHA across every local repository and filtered to
my exact author identity. They measure directed, reviewed, and integrated
engineering — not a claim that I typed every line.

Unique commits per month: Aug 589 · Sep 138 · Oct 2 · Nov 940 · Dec 1,113 ·
Jan 1,028 · Feb 1,286 · Mar 591 · Apr 1,505 · May 3,196 · Jun 4,008 ·
Jul 3,314 (first twelve days). October is real, too: two commits. The pace was
sustained, not retrofitted.

## The research programs

Every program below is a running system with its own tests, documents, and Git
history. Four satellites follow, and the repository archive on the page holds
the rest.

### Faber / Radix — language / compiler (active, private)

A Latin-inspired programming language and Radix, its Rust compiler. Shared
parsing and typechecking feed two lanes — one lowers to reviewable Rust and
native binaries, the other to runtime artifacts — with emission targets across
Go, TypeScript, WebAssembly, LLVM, Metal, and WGSL. Built through 219
documented factory initiatives, each with its own goals, ledgers, and
acceptance audits.

5,512 commits · 2,918 test definitions · 219 factory initiatives
Site: https://www.faberlang.dev · Org: https://github.com/faberlang ·
Grammar: https://github.com/ianzepp/tree-sitter-faber

### Minted Geek Swarm — agent runtime (active, private)

A Rust runtime monorepo built around one daemon, swarmd: fifteen domain
crates — kernel, filesystem, MCP, messaging, payments — behind a single public
HTTP boundary. Internal work moves over kernel frames, and black-box suites
drive the built binary through the same routes users hit.

1,928 commits since May · 1,262 test definitions · ~97% Rust
Site: https://www.mintedgeek.com · the GitHub org is private

### Field Board — seven-day build (open source)

A real-time collaborative whiteboard with AI board manipulation, written in
Rust end to end: Axum and PostgreSQL behind, Leptos and WebAssembly in front,
binary protobuf frames between. Seven crates in seven days, February 2026.

511 commits · 1,077 test definitions · 7 crates / 7 days
Source: https://github.com/ianzepp/gauntlet-week-1

### The Trials — evaluation science (open + private)

Harnesses for asking whether models can actually learn Faber — grammar-only
versus worked examples, n-shot matrices, three-level executable grading, judged
drafter-and-reviewer pipelines — plus local-inference tuning, ethics-scenario
designs, and blind design judging. One January study ran four models through
672 trials each.

17,681 result rows · 26 models · 266 task definitions
Harness: https://github.com/ianzepp/faber-trials

### Monk — programmable platform (open source)

A multi-tenant backend where the schema is data: model-first APIs, per-tenant
isolation, observer rings, packages, cron — and protocol adapters that expose
the same records over FUSE, FTP, and IRC. The clearest bridge between my
enterprise-platform years and the current work.

1,122 commits · 15+ ecosystem repos
Source: https://github.com/ianzepp/monk-api

### The kernel lineage — agent kernels (mixed)

A line of experiments in how agents should execute: Abbot's persistent daemon,
Prior's typed frames and kernel routing, Muninn's polyglot protocol family,
Fleet's Mind/Head/Hand orchestration — plus Cassio for transcript processing
and Vivarium for email as a durable agent data surface.

6 related systems · Rust / TS / Go cores
Abbot: https://github.com/ianzepp/abbot · Cassio: https://github.com/ianzepp/cassio

### Satellites

- **Cephalopodic** (MCP security, collaborative): a Go control plane and
  inline security gateway for MCP: registration, catalogs, user-scoped taps,
  and Fortress inspecting JSON-RPC with quarantine and policy enforcement.
- **Gofolio** (applied product): a Ghostfolio-compatible portfolio backend in
  Go, a Rust terminal client, and a live evaluation TUI running 73 defined
  cases across models with executable grading.
  https://github.com/ianzepp/gofolio-cli
- **LegacyLens** (applied AI): retrieval-augmented analysis of legacy COBOL:
  custom parsing and chunking, vector indexing, hybrid retrieval, and
  natural-language answers over a real mainframe codebase.
  https://github.com/ianzepp/legacylens
- **QRStatic** (research crate): zero-dependency Rust steganography hiding QR
  codes in temporal noise correlation, with empirical codec, quantization, and
  recovery sweeps behind the defaults. https://github.com/ianzepp/qrstatic

## The operating method: how the factory runs

Reconstructed from 9,588 archived session transcripts, this is the loop on most
days, across most systems. The agents supply throughput. The judgment stays
human.

1. **Write the goal first.** The intended end state and its invariants go into
   a document that outlives the conversation. So far: 216 goal documents, 43
   campaign plans, 91 ledgers.
2. **Split into bounded phases.** Parallel agents get non-overlapping scopes.
   Read-only scouts go ahead of architecture changes; worktrees isolate
   anything that might collide.
3. **Implement one coherent slice.** Format, lint, test, inspect the diff — in
   that order, every time. Weak tests and policy evasion get rejected, not
   merged.
4. **Commit as punctuation.** A commit is a cognitive checkpoint between design
   and the next phase, not an end-of-day dump.
5. **Audit separately.** Correctness, security, performance, and documentation
   each get their own pass — and goal completion is judged apart from
   implementation completion.

The division of labor:

- **My job:** pick the problem and the invariant. Challenge the architecture
  and the naming. Decide clean-break versus compatibility. Partition the
  parallel work, test outcomes independently, and decide when the evidence is
  sufficient.
- **The agents' job:** reconnaissance, implementation throughput, review
  passes, documentation, and the repetitive transformations nobody should do by
  hand.

In May 2026, one goal produced seven committed phases and separate acceptance
proofs — and an audit that *refused to call the goal complete* while recovery
requirements remained open. That refusal is the point.

Document counts: 216 goals · 43 campaigns · 1,396 delivery docs · 91 ledgers.

## The skill library

Over the last six months, these repo-owned skills have grown into a cohesive
layer of systems-engineering automation with one design goal: make the LLM's
job easier. Nearly every session on this page ran through them.

- **/fleet** — the newest, and a favorite: Mind, Head, and Hand roles for
  multi-agent project loops, with stewardship and dead-man continuation. Built
  on Vivi mailspaces, so agents coordinate over mail instead of shared memory.
- **/campaign · /factory · /delivery** — the work-flow spine, used on
  practically everything. Campaigns and sub-campaigns organize the flow of
  work; a factory defines the phases for each unit; every phase gets a ledger
  that tracks it to completion.
- **/polish** — a per-file improvement loop backed by a deterministic analyzer
  that moves judgment calls out of the model and into repeatable checks. Polish
  is what keeps boilerplate LLM code from becoming slop.
- **/housekeeping** — repository hygiene with ratchets: not all code is
  perfect, so exceptions are explicit — and get ratcheted up or down per repo
  as the code earns it. This is how a codebase stays in clean, competent form.
- **/cassio** — the skill behind the evidence on this page. Converts Claude,
  Codex, and OpenCode sessions into readable Markdown transcripts — and
  extracts training data for customized LLM tuning.
- **/mail + Vivi** — arbitrary local mailspaces for agents and projects. Vivi
  grew out of the mail skill and became the substrate Fleet coordinates over —
  private email treated as durable agent infrastructure.

Supporting skills: /warmup, /goal-forge, /goal-check, /correctness,
/cleanliness, /consequences, /root-cause, /red-green, /bonsai, /clean-break,
/zombie-docs, /poker-face, /optimization, /caretaker, /dealers-choice,
/skill-author, /slice, /scrum, /transcripts, /trials, /deploy, /docs, and more.

All of it points one direction. The same principle that shaped these skills is
the founding premise of Faber: a language designed for LLMs first, because
humans don't write the code anymore — we just need to be able to understand
what's going on.

## The backstory: a career in four acts

Four acts, dated from executed agreements, payroll records, and public archives
where those exist. The evidence ledger below says so when they don't.

### Act I — 1996—2009: Rifles, then a KDE front end for Nmap.

Four years in the Marine Corps — 0351 Assaultman, out as a Corporal with an
honorable discharge — left me with a bias toward responsibility that never wore
off. In January 2000 I released KMap, a C++/Qt front end for Nmap. The Nmap
2.50 release notes mention it by name, which is still my favorite line of
third-party evidence.

The path from there was not direct: five years selling real estate in Florida
before joining Beatport's API team in Denver in 2008, where electronic music
distribution ran on Zend PHP, enterprise Java, Mule, Spring, Hibernate, Squid,
Akamai, and MySQL.

USMC / 0351 / E-4 · C++ / Qt / KDE · PHP / Java

### Act II — 2009—2017: Salesforce, scale, and the founder turn.

At Red Hat I worked on a multilingual APAC Partner Center built on
Salesforce — Korea, Japan, and China, twenty-odd sandboxes. roundCorner hired
me in 2011 as Chief Scientist; by the end I was VP Engineering, and the team
had grown from four people to twelve, spread across four continents.

In 2014 I founded Minted.IO and spent 2015 self-funding a metadata-driven
platform and API business. After a year inside Salesforce as a Technical
Solution Architect, Motivis acquired the Minted.IO assets in February 2017. My
VP offer was written into the acquisition.

Chief Scientist → VP Eng · Team 4 → 12 · Founder / acquired

### Act III — 2017—2024: Platform leadership, then enough.

At Motivis I ran platform R&D — roughly ten engineers on a TypeScript, Node.js,
PostgreSQL, and Google Cloud learning platform — then shifted to independent
architecture and strategy consulting through Minted Geek, my Estonian company,
from 2019.

By 2021 I stopped taking work. Early retirement was a genuine attempt to be
finished with the industry, and for about four years, it held.

VP Platform R&D · TS / Node / GCP · Minted Geek OÜ

### Act IV — 2025—NOW: The tools changed. I came back.

In August 2025 I pulled two decades of old source out of storage — KMap, the
Motivis-era platform, payment systems — and started committing again. In
October I barely touched a keyboard: two commits. Then November arrived, and
with it the start of a 117-day unbroken streak.

What it became is the lab described above: a language and its compiler, two
runtimes, a platform, security tooling, and thousands of recorded trials
measuring whether any of it actually works. The receipts are in the ledger
below.

Rust / Go / TypeScript · Compilers / agents / MCP · 17,710 commits

## The evidence ledger

Old résumés are memory. This history has been reconstructed against executed
agreements, employment records, public archives, source code, Git history, and
thousands of AI-session transcripts. Sensitive documents remain private; their
claims do not. Where the record is thin, the grade says so.

Grades: **A** = directly verified (executed records, primary sources) ·
**B** = corroborated (first-person record plus a credible second source) ·
**C** = first-person recollection, not yet independently confirmed.

- **1996—2000 · United States Marine Corps — grade A.** A DD-214 records
  active service from May 1996 to May 2000, an honorable discharge, the rank of
  Corporal (E-4), and the 0351 Assaultman occupational specialty.
- **2000 · KMap enters the Nmap ecosystem — grade A.** Nmap's contemporary
  release announcement names "a KDE front end by Ian Zepp"; the mailing-list
  archive preserves my KMap 0.7 announcement, Linux and FreeBSD notes included.
  https://insecure.org/stf/Nmap-2.50-Release.html ·
  https://seclists.org/nmap-announce/2000/1
- **2008—09 · Beatport engineering — grade A.** Employer records — payroll,
  benefits, and a 2008 performance review — establish the software-development
  role. The detailed stack narrative comes from my own résumé of the period,
  and is labeled accordingly.
- **2009 · Red Hat architecture work — grade C.** Two consistent historical
  résumés describe the APAC Partner Center work, and an RHCE certification fits
  the period — but no employer-issued record has surfaced yet. So this entry
  stays a C, and stays labeled.
- **2011—15 · roundCorner leadership — grade B.** An executed employment
  agreement, equity records, and separation correspondence establish the
  relationship and the Chief Scientist start. Public business records
  corroborate the later VP Engineering title; the exact promotion dates remain
  unresolved.
  https://www.gaebler.com/Funded-Company-0F5780A5-FE79-4BE4-B38A-753CAE0641D0-roundCorner
- **2016—17 · Salesforce employment — grade A.** An executed offer for
  Technical Solution Architect and a continuous payroll record from February
  2016 through February 2017 establish employment. The deeper client and
  architecture narrative comes from contemporaneous career records.
- **2017 · Minted.IO acquired by Motivis — grade A.** The executed
  asset-purchase agreement describes the acquired business as software-platform
  and API development. A linked employment offer — expressly conditioned on the
  acquisition closing — brought me into Motivis as VP, Platform Research and
  Development.
- **2025—26 · Independent AI research at repository scale — grade A.** Local
  and authenticated GitHub inventories cover 218 repositories. Git histories,
  structured transcript archives, trial-result stores, and factory documents
  provide dated, inspectable evidence for individual systems and decisions —
  measured, most recently, on July 12, 2026. https://github.com/ianzepp

step. The repository archive on the page is generated from live GitHub data;
everything around it is hand-authored.
